title: codec churn microburst skyline scratchpad
content:
Purpose: quick working notes from the mini-bench run that tried enabling dynamic codec switching (lz4 -> zstd-level4 -> zstd-level1 fallbacks) during minute-scale microbursts. Goal was to measure p50/p90/p99 latency impact and CPU spillover + egress delta across codecs and transition churn.

Background / why this matters:
- Console payload compression was added to reduce token egress $/byte during sustained chat workloads.
- We saw smaller-than-expected savings during microbursts: hypothesis is codec churn (switching/negotiation + rebuffering) creates short-lived latency spikes and CPU overhead that kills p99.
- This round of runs instrumented codec transitions and measured latency envelopes and cost delta in the hot path.

Hypotheses tested:
1) Dynamic codec switching on per-request basis increases p99 due to extra negotiation + small re-encode windows.
2) Keeping a per-tenant sticky codec with opportunistic shift at 30s boundary reduces churn and recovers p99 at modest egress cost.
3) Lower compression (zstd-level1) during spikes reduces CPU tail and p99 even if bytes up ~8-12%.

Test setup (short):
- Cluster: demo-dedicated-GPU-pool-3 (4 x A100s), proxy nodes on c6i.8xlarge for compression ops.
- Workload: synthetic chat sessions (2k concurrent sessions), baseline session length = 45 tokens generation average, burst profile: 60s ramp to 2.5x QPS, hold 30s, decay 90s.
- Codecs: none (raw), lz4-framed, zstd-lvl1, zstd-lvl4. Dynamic-switch policy: start zstd4; if CPU>70% for 5s switch to zstd1; if mem pressure + latency > p90 threshold then fallback to none for 10s.
- Observed metrics: request-latency-ms (p50/p90/p99), codec-transitions/sec, compress-cpu-percent (proxy), egress-bytes, inferred $egress (rough $0.00045/MB for example account), cost-per-minute estimate.

Run summary (aggregated 6 runs, short hand):
- baseline (none): p50 34ms / p90 108ms / p99 420ms; egress 100% (100 MB/min baseline cost unit). CPU proxy low.
- lz4 sticky: p50 37ms / p90 115ms / p99 480ms; egress -12% ; CPU +8% (spike harmless).
- zstd4 dynamic: p50 40ms / p90 150ms / p99 920ms (!); egress -28% ; codec-transitions peaked at 180/min; compress-cpu jumped +45% during transition windows.
- zstd1 sticky: p50 38ms / p90 120ms / p99 510ms; egress -18% ; CPU +20%.

Text charts (ascii) - p99 timeline (example run):
Time(s) | p99 ms
0       | 410
30      | 430
60      | 460
90      | 880  <-- burst+codec-transitions spike
120     | 520
150     | 450
180     | 430

Spike sparkline p99: ▁▁▁▁▂▇▃▂

Codec transitions/sec (zstd4 dynamic run) ascii: ▁▂▂▅▆▇▇▇▆▅▂▁ (peak at center)

Cost rough delta table (minute-averages, normalized):
strategy,egress(bytes/min,normalized),egress-$,cpu-proxy-avg(%),p99(ms)
none,1.00,$0.00045,12,420
lz4-sticky,0.88,$0.00040,13,480
zstd4-dynamic,0.72,$0.00032,18,920
zstd1-sticky,0.82,$0.00037,14,510

Key observations / takeaways:
- Dynamic switching to zstd-level4 reduces egress cost (~28%) but introduces severe p99 regressions during the burst transition window. The regression correlates tightly with codec-transitions/sec and compress-cpu spikes.
- Sticky lower-level (zstd1) gives a better tradeoff: reasonable egress reduction while keeping p99 within ~20% of baseline.
- LZ4 sticky is CPU-cheaper than zstd4 and avoids the massive p99 jump; egress savings modest.
- The worst-case p99 behavior looks like a queuing spike in the proxy compression thread pool when transitions happen concurrently across many sessions.

Quick root-cause notes (working):
- Transition path includes: detect -> flush partial frames -> negotiate new framing headers -> allocate encode buffer -> re-encode tail tokens. These happen per-session and are blocking on a shared encode pool; when many sessions align, we saturate the encode pool and latency spikes.
- Memory churn from zstd dictionary allocations also observed (short-lived) causing GC-like pauses on proxy process (we're in Rust, so actually allocator stall, but effect similar).

Experiment ideas to mitigate (next runs):
- Per-tenant sticky codec with TTL (30s-120s) so we only shift at coarse boundaries. Expect to drop transitions/sec dramatically.
- Staggered transition windows (per shard) to avoid global alignment: pick random 0-8s jitter on transition decision.
- Increase encode pool size and make encode queue preemptible for high-priority streaming requests. Measure CPU cost and latency tradeoff.
- Try hybrid: pre-encode prefixes for likely next chunk (prefetch encode) and then compress rest lazily.
- Telemetry: add per-session encode-queue-time metric and encode-pool-saturation gauge.

Action items (owners):
- (Maya) schedule next run with per-tenant sticky + 0-12s jitter, add encode-queue-time metric. target: 2029-06-22.
- (Jon) prototype a thin pre-encode prefix cache for session tails (P0 experimental).
- (Lena) run memory/allocation profiler on proxy during transition to pinpoint allocator hotspots.
- (Priya) add Linear tickets for rollout gating and SLO notes.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How sensitive is p99 to encode pool size vs codec CPU cost? need sweep.
- Should we expose a per-route codec control in console or keep heuristic internal? product call pending.
- Cost model: are egress savings worth the p99 risk for small-enterprise customers vs larger ones? need customer cohort mapping.

References and links in run notes:
- linear: RED-1247 (investigation)
- github: realtime-proto PR #489 (codec negotiation change)
- slack: #encode-team thread (link in linked_artifacts)

Notes to self: keep doc rough. This is more of a bench scratchpad than a polished brief. Will distill into a one-pager if sticky-per-tenant + jitter shows meaningful improvement (expected).

End of scratchpad.
